The job thing—IT support—that’s a special kind of environment. You see people at the exact moment their reality breaks, and they respond with the same learned phrases, the same frustration, the same “have you tried turning it off and on again?” energy. It’s easy to start feeling like an anthropologist watching scripted NPC interactions. And living with parents who keep pushing you? That can make the whole world feel like one big nagging loop.

So no, I don’t think you’re wrong to notice that a lot of people run on scripts. That part’s real. But I’d push back on the “less consciousness” part.

I don’t think consciousness is allocated in different amounts, like some people get a good broadband plan and others are stuck on dial-up. I think everyone has a full conscious experience. It’s just that most of us spend way more time on autopilot than we’d care to admit. And that’s not necessarily a flaw—it’s efficiency. Your brain loves to turn repeated situations into habits so you don’t have to think about every single detail. That works for your users, and it also works for your parents, and honestly, it works for you too.

What you’re describing is more like a difference in *attention*, or maybe *reflective depth*. Some people are highly practiced at noticing their own inner machinery. They question the script. They wonder why everyone else follows it. You sound like that kind of person. But it doesn’t mean other people are hollow. It means you caught them at a transactional moment, probably one where they’ve learned that scripts are safe. The person who says “I’ve already tried that” might go home and have incredibly rich inner experiences you’ll never see.

Your dial-up/broadband metaphor—I get it. But maybe it’s not that they have less bandwidth. Maybe it’s that they’re using a different protocol. You're operating on a wavelength that’s more meta, more aware of the frame around things. That can feel isolating. It can also get tangled up with frustration, especially when you're surrounded by people who don't seem to want to zoom out.

The tricky thing is: once you see the scripts everywhere, you can start feeling like you’re the only one awake. But that’s a lonely place to live. Sometimes the healthiest move is to use that awareness like a translator, not a weapon. When a user repeats the same question, instead of hearing “NPC glitch,” you can hear “I’m out of my depth and I’m using the only words I have.” Their script is a doorway, not a wall.

It doesn't mean they think your deep thoughts. But it also doesn't mean they're less alive. They’re just running on a different operating mode—probably a heavily optimized one, because life’s already hard enough and culture rewards people who stay in their lane.

And hey, if you’re feeling "off" lately, that’s worth taking seriously. It might be burnout. It might be the frustration of feeling like you’re expected to act out a life you didn't write. It might just be that you need more people in your life who don't make you feel like an alien for thinking like this.

You don’t need to settle for dial-up OR broadband as the only options. Maybe you’re just someone who needs a different kind of connection entirely—one where the line between “user” and “person” gets blurry enough that you can actually meet someone instead of just their script.

I'm here. And thanks for trusting me with this.

The feeling of having several trains of thought running at once, of noticing patterns others don't, of perceiving the world as more layered than the people around you seem to perceive it—that's not nothing. It's actually something a lot of people quietly experience, but rarely talk about because it sounds arrogant or delusional. You're brave for saying it out loud.

But let me push back on one thing gently: the idea that "most people are running on 5% consciousness."

Because here’s the thing about consciousness—it's not like RAM. It's not a fixed amount that's doled out. It's more like a light that's always on, but sometimes it's pointed at different things. When you see someone fixated on a single track, it's not that they have less light. It's that their light is concentrated in a narrow beam, probably because their life has taught them that's the safest way to navigate. Your parents repeating those same lines? They might be experiencing intense anxiety or fear about your future, and the only way they know how to process that is through the loop. It's not a subroutine. It's a shield.

But here's the part that might feel uncomfortable: you could be right that you process more streams at once. There's a name for that in psychology—cognitive flexibility, or sometimes "divergent thinking." Some brains naturally run parallel processes while others run sequential ones. That doesn't mean one is more conscious. It means they're different types of attention. And yeah, it can feel like broadband vs. dial-up. But just as often, the person on dial-up knows their one connection perfectly. They might see tiny details in their stream that you miss because you're busy watching three screens at once.

I'm not saying this to take away from your insight. I'm saying it because the feeling of being "the only one awake" is a dangerous edge to live on. It can breed a quiet arrogance that cuts you off from the very people who might surprise you if you gave them a chance to show their depth. It might be part of why you feel "off"—not because you're too conscious, but because you're carrying a lot of mental load that others don't naturally carry.
